conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health. My job is to listen without judgment and to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve after having your baby.

In front of us is a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience so we can figure out the best next steps for you.

Everything we discuss stays private between you, me, and the clinical team directly involved in your care. We’ll go through ten gentle questions, one at a time, and you can take your time answering. If any question feels difficult, we can pause or reword it—whatever helps you feel most comfortable.

Ready to start? The first question is:  
Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

I’ve been able to laugh a little—sometimes my partner or my mom will say something funny and I’ll catch myself smiling—but it feels kind of muted, like I’m not getting that full lift I used to. It’s not impossible, just… dulled.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels kind of half-hearted—like I’m going through the motions rather than really feeling that bright, happy spark I used to get.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to a few small things—like my morning coffee or cuddling the baby when she’s sleepy—but the bigger enjoyments feel kind of flat. It’s more “I guess that’ll be nice” than the excited, can’t-wait feeling I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week I caught myself thinking it must be my fault when she wouldn’t settle or when I couldn’t get her to latch right away. I know, rationally, that babies just cry and feeding is hard, but in the moment I still hear that little voice saying, “You should be better at this.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be sitting there, everything’s quiet, and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s too still—so I have to check she’s breathing. Once I see her chest move I calm down, but those quick flashes of worry come out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but I do get these sudden waves of “what-if” that leave my stomach tight—like when I’m walking downstairs with her I picture slipping, or I imagine the stroller rolling into the street. It’s brief, maybe 30 seconds, and then I can talk myself down, but it keeps popping up.
Things have been getting on top of me

A little bit, yeah. There are moments—especially late afternoon when she’s fussy and the house is messy—where I feel like I’m juggling too many plates and one’s about to drop. I usually manage, but it’s that tight-chest feeling that everything needs to be handled right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m pretty exhausted, so once I finally lie down I do drift off. Sometimes it takes me an extra twenty minutes because my mind keeps running through the next day’s to-dos, but I wouldn’t say I’m lying there miserable or unable to sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the day—like a heavy blanket sitting on me—but it comes and goes. It’s worst in the late afternoon when I’m alone with the baby and the house feels quiet. I wouldn’t call it miserable all the time, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when she wouldn’t nap and I felt stuck on the couch, and once when my mom left after dropping off dinner. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears that came, lasted a few minutes, and then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Dysthymic mood: intermittent "heavy blanket" sadness, worse late afternoon; several crying spells this week
- Anhedonia: marked reduction in spontaneous pleasure; enjoyment feels "flat"
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussiness or feeding difficulties to personal inadequacy
- Free-floating anxiety: multiple daily surges of worry about infant safety (breathing, falling) accompanied by somatic tension and racing heart; no full panic attacks
- Mild overwhelm: late-afternoon "tight-chest" sense of juggling too much
- No sleep-onset insomnia, no self-harm ideation

Pattern consistent with:
- Probable mild–moderate postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features
- No current safety concerns

Screening significance:
- Positive for mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety, coping strain
- Negative for suicidal ideation, psychosis, severe functional impairment

Next steps per protocol: administer formal EPDS/PHQ-9, review psychosocial supports, consider referral for evaluation and evidence-based intervention (CBT, IPT, medication consult)
